pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9, Geography & Local Weather — different places have very different typical weather (tropics hot/wet, deserts dry, poles freezing) and geography (distance from the Equator, altitude, nearness to the sea) drives those differences.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1/KS2 geography — identify hot and cold areas of the world in relation to the Equator and the North/South Poles; describe and understand climate zones.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-ESS2-2 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-2]' — the direct anchor. State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: teach latitude (distance from the Equator) as the dominant control, then layer secondary factors (altitude cools; the sea moderates); use a globe/map so children can locate places and read the Equator-to-pole temperature gradient; combine information from maps, photos and data (aligning to 3-ESS2-2's 'obtain and combine').
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — describe typical weather in three climate types and state that places near the Equator are hotter; Tier B — name a non-latitude factor (altitude/sea) and explain its effect; Tier C — combine multiple factors to explain a specific place's climate.
bestPractices: Establish latitude first — the Equator-to-pole temperature gradient — using a globe so the Sun-angle cause is spatially anchored
Add one factor at a time (altitude cools even at the Equator; nearness to the sea evens out temperatures) so children can isolate causes
Have children 'obtain and combine' information from at least two sources (map + climate data or photos) to meet 3-ESS2-2
Compare concrete, contrasting places (rainforest, hot desert, polar) with vivid imagery and data
Confront the 'south = always hot' hemisphere confusion by comparing places at similar latitudes north and south
keyRepresentations: A globe/world map with latitude bands shaded by typical temperature (Equator warm → poles cold)
Factor toggles: latitude, altitude, distance-to-sea, each changing a place's typical weather
Contrasting climate photo/data cards (tropical, desert, temperate, polar, mountain)
An 'up a mountain' inset showing cooling with altitude at a fixed latitude
commonMisconceptions: Latitude is the only thing that matters — altitude and nearness to the sea also strongly shape local weather
'The South is always hot / the North is always cold' — ignores hemispheres and that both poles are cold
Mountains near the Equator must be hot — high altitude makes them cold despite low latitude
Deserts are always hot — some (e.g. polar/high deserts) are cold; 'desert' means dry, not hot
Weather in a place is random rather than shaped by predictable geographic factors

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, help children see that a place's typical weather is not random but shaped by a few predictable geographic causes: distance from the Equator (latitude) is the main control on temperature, with altitude (higher is generally colder) and nearness to the sea (which usually evens out hot and cold extremes and can bring moisture) as major secondary factors. Children first establish the Equator-to-pole temperature gradient, then isolate one factor at a time, 'obtain and combine' information from at least two sources (map plus climate data or photos), and confront common confusions such as 'the South is always hot', 'higher means hotter', and 'all deserts are hot'.

activities.title: Climate map: vary one cause at a time
feedback: If a child says a mountain on the Equator must be hot, point to mountaintop-snow photos and prompt: the air high up is thinner and holds less heat, so higher is colder even near the Equator (an age-appropriate gloss of the fuller physics).
If a child expects two same-latitude places to have identical weather, have them change only ONE factor (altitude OR distance to sea) and watch the weather diverge.
When a child reads the sea as only cooling or only warming, show it both ways: cooler summers AND milder winters compared with inland places at the same latitude.
Affirm correct reasoning by asking the child to name which single factor they changed and what effect it had.
activities.rationale: The target is cause-and-effect: geography drives climate. Letting a child vary one driver at a time and see the typical weather change supports the 'obtain and combine information to describe climates' move, and isolating factors counters single-factor thinking. Live readouts, a draggable latitude marker, and altitude/coast toggles are optional interaction examples that make the causal mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Latitude is the dominant control on climate, with altitude and proximity to the sea as major secondary factors; children commonly over-attribute climate to latitude alone.
learnerActions: Drop a place-marker somewhere on a world map and read its typical weather (e.g. typical temperature and whether it is wet or dry).
Drag the marker from the poles toward the Equator and describe the overall trend in temperature along the way (watch for places, like high mountains, that break the pattern).

Park a place on the Equator at low altitude (hot all year), then raise its ALTITUDE and describe what happens to its weather; then move a place next to the sea and describe how its hot/cold extremes change.
Combine a map view with a climate data or photo card into a short spoken or written summary: 'This place is ___ because ___.'
activities.intendedInsight: A place's weather is the combined effect of a few geographic causes you can switch on and off: latitude sets the baseline, altitude cools, and the sea evens out extremes.

activities.title: Spinning globe: why the Equator is hotter
feedback: If a child says the South is always hot and the North always cold, compare both poles (both freezing) and places at similar latitudes north and south of the Equator.
Reinforce that 'near the Equator = more direct sun = warmer' by having the child point to where the beam is most concentrated.
activities.rationale: A rotatable globe makes the Equator-to-pole gradient genuinely spatial and can show the Sun-angle cause behind it, which a flat map represents less directly. A flat map can still teach the gradient; the globe is offered for the deeper 'why', not as the only way to learn this. The movable sunlight beam and latitude-band overlay are optional interaction examples. Note: the direct-vs-glancing-sunlight mechanism is correct science but is not directly stated in the listed sources.
learnerActions: Rotate a globe and locate the Equator and the North and South Poles.
Shine a movable sunlight beam onto the globe and compare how directly the rays strike near the Equator versus near the poles.
Explain in your own words why places near the Equator tend to be hotter, using the idea of direct versus glancing sunlight.
activities.intendedInsight: The Equator is hotter because sunlight hits it more directly, while it strikes the poles at a glancing angle — a spatial cause for the temperature gradient.

activities.title: Compare contrasting real places
feedback: If a child assumes every desert is hot, show a cold/high desert example and clarify that desert means dry.
If sequencing ignores altitude, include a cold place near the Equator as a deliberate trap and ask what factor overrides latitude there.
activities.rationale: Comparing concrete, vivid, contrasting places with both imagery and data supports describing typical weather across climate types and 'obtaining and combining' information from more than one source. A sort/sequence can check and reinforce classification but does not by itself require the child to produce an explanation, so it is paired with a spoken/written reason. The altitude 'trap' (a cold place at low latitude) surfaces the misconception that latitude is the only control.
learnerActions: Study photo and climate-data cards for contrasting places: a tropical rainforest, a hot desert, a temperate coast, a polar region, and a high mountain.
Describe the typical weather of at least three of these climate types in your own words.
Sort or sequence the places from coldest to hottest and say which geographic factor best explains each place's weather.
Explain how a cold desert or a cold high desert can be a 'desert' — point out that 'desert' means dry, not hot.
activities.intendedInsight: Different places have very different typical weather, and for each case children can name a geographic factor (latitude, altitude, or nearness to the sea) that helps explain it, while knowing other things such as winds and mountains blocking rain also play a part.

activities.title: Same latitude, different weather (diagnostic discussion)
feedback: Gap response ('same latitude must mean same weather'): compare paired places that differ in only ONE factor at a time.
Partial response (lists altitude/sea/wind but can't isolate which explains a given difference): ask which single factor separates these two specific towns.

Full response: the child explains local weather as the combined effect of altitude, distance from the sea and wind, and isolates the operative factor for a new paired case such as equatorial mountain snow.
activities.rationale: Holding latitude constant between two towns forces beyond-latitude reasoning and discriminates single-factor thinkers from children who can hold and isolate multiple factors. Spoken, responsive discussion lets a teacher probe and reteach in the moment.
sourceClaims: Latitude is the dominant control on climate, with altitude and proximity to the sea as major secondary factors; children commonly over-attribute climate to latitude alone.
learnerActions: Consider two towns at the same distance from the Equator on the same day and time of year: one high on a mountain, one by the sea. Explain why their weather might be quite different.
Answer: which single factor would you change to make the mountain town's weather more like the coastal town's?
Discuss: it snows on a mountain in a hot country near the Equator — how can that be?
Discuss: why do coastal places often have milder winters than inland places at the same latitude?
activities.intendedInsight: When latitude is held equal, you must appeal to other factors — altitude, nearness to the sea, wind — to explain a difference, and you can isolate which factor is doing the work.

activities.title: Voices from contrasting climates (enrichment)
feedback: If a child enjoys the story but can't name a cause, return to the map or globe to pin down the latitude/altitude/sea factor for that place.
Prompt the child to compare two accounts and say which geographic factor explains the difference.
activities.rationale: Interviews or first-person accounts can humanise the topic and aid engagement, but the spatial cause-and-effect may be more directly anchored on a map or globe than through narration alone; this activity is an enrichment companion, not the primary route to the causal concept.
learnerActions: Read or listen to short accounts from people living in contrasting climates (e.g. tropical, desert, polar, mountain) describing their typical weather and daily life.
Match each account to its climate type and name the geographic factor that most shapes that place's weather.
activities.intendedInsight: Real human experiences can make distant climates vivid and relatable, and each can be tied back to the geographic causes behind that place's weather.

constraints: Children must 'obtain and combine' information from at least two sources (e.g. map plus climate data or photos) to meet the describe-climates objective, which explicitly calls for combining information; a single source does not satisfy that objective.

A tap-to-reveal labelled map can convey 'different places, different weather' but does not let a child isolate latitude vs altitude vs sea; use it as an introductory scaffold rather than the means to teach the causal core.

Recognition tasks (matching, sequencing, multiple choice) can assess and reinforce classification but do not by themselves require the child to construct an explanation; pair them with a spoken or written explanation of why a place has its weather.
Teach latitude first, then add only one secondary factor at a time (altitude, then sea) so children can isolate each cause.

A globe represents the spherical Earth more spatially than a flat map; a flat map is a flattened representation of the sphere but can still show the Equator-to-pole gradient. Distinguish the real spherical Earth from any flat picture or digital model of it; globes and maps on screen or card are models, not the Earth itself.
Explicitly confront hemisphere confusion ('South = always hot') by comparing places at similar latitudes north and south, and note that both poles are cold.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three sources (DfE curriculum claim; the latitude/altitude/sea dominance claim) are marked unverified in the source row; treat their specific framings as unconfirmed.

The original row implied a flat map 'cannot' show the Equator-to-pole cause and that 2D toggles are 'ideal'; these comparative/necessity claims are catalog preferences, not established efficacy findings, and have been softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances.

The direct-vs-glancing-sunlight mechanism in the globe activity is correct, age-appropriate science but is not directly supported by any of the three listed sources (its sourceClaims is therefore empty); the DfE claim supports only the locate-Equator/poles portion.
Comparative medium claims (map/globe better than narration; human accounts aiding memorability) are plausible but untested and have been softened to may/proposed wording.

Simplifications for ages 7–9: 'thinner air holds less heat' is a child-level gloss of why higher altitude is colder (the full explanation involves pressure and adiabatic effects); and 'latitude is the dominant control' is a general tendency, not a universal rule. Keep these as age-appropriate approximations and avoid overstating them.

probeDeeper: Which single factor would you change to make the mountain town's weather more like the coastal town's?
It snows on a mountain in a hot country near the equator. How can that be?
Why do coastal places often have milder winters than inland places at the same latitude?
assess.correctAnswer: Factors besides latitude shape local weather: altitude (higher is colder), nearness to the sea (the ocean moderates temperature and adds moisture), and things like prevailing wind and mountains. So the same latitude can still mean very different local weather.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The only thing that changes weather is how far north you are' — single-factor thinking
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare paired places that differ in only ONE factor at a time.
errorPatterns.distractor: They should have the same weather because they're the same distance from the equator.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: gives a one-factor answer and is stuck when latitude is held equal

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Higher up is warmer because it's closer to the Sun'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mountaintop-snow photos; thinner air holds less heat, so higher is colder.
errorPatterns.distractor: The mountain town is warmer because it's nearer the Sun.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts the mountain town is hotter

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The sea makes a place colder (or hotter) all the time' — treats the coast as one-directional
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the sea moderates — cooler summers AND milder winters.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes the sea's effect as only cooling or only warming

responseLevels.gap: Says the same latitude must mean the same weather; single-factor thinking.
responseLevels.full: Explains local weather as the combined effect of altitude, distance from the sea and wind, and isolates the operative factor for a new paired case such as equatorial mountain snow.
responseLevels.partial: Lists factors (altitude, sea, wind) but cannot isolate which one explains a specific difference between the two towns.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two towns are at the same distance from the equator on the same day and time of year. One sits high on a mountain, the other by the sea. Why might their weather be quite different?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks only 'how far north/south' or 'how sunny' sets weather cannot explain a difference between same-latitude towns; only a child holding multiple factors can isolate why the mountain and coastal towns differ.
